summary_html: Agency or actor engages in **discriminatory or retaliatory action**, violating civil-rights or placement-equality provisions. Federal statutes prohibit race, religion, sex, or disability bias in placements or investigations.
authority_html:
- **Multiethnic Placement Act (MEPA) & Interethnic Adoption Provisions (IEP)** — prohibits race/ethnicity discrimination in placements  
- **Civil Rights Act (42 U.S.C. § 2000d)** — Title VI discrimination prohibitions in federally funded programs

primary_citations.citation_text: New Mexico - NMSA 1978 Chapter 32A, Article 4 (Abuse and Neglect Act: 32A-4-3 duty to report, 32A-4-18 custody hearings, 32A-4-19 adjudicatory hearings), CYFD-published Children's Code compilation (2023 text; 32A-4-3 amended 2025 by SB 42)

New Mexico Statutes Chapter 27 - Public Assistance (public assistance and Medicaid programs; CYFD's child-welfare authority is not in this chapter — it is the Children, Youth and Families Department Act, NMSA 1978 § 9-2A-7(D), and the Children's Code, NMSA 1978 § 32A-1-1, per 8.10.3.3 NMAC)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: State ex rel. Children, Youth & Families Department v. Christina L.
key_cases.holding: The court reversed a neglect adjudication, holding that the district court's findings did not establish that a mental disorder or incapacity was the cause of the mother's inability to care for the child as Section 32A-4-2(E)(4) requires.
key_cases.relevance: It bars treating a parent's disability as neglect without proof of a causal link, the core anti-disability-discrimination protection in New Mexico adjudications.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that the district court's findings do not support a determination that Child was neglected pursuant to NMSA 1978, § 32A-4-2(E)(4) (2009)

key_cases.case_name: State ex rel. Children, Youth & Families Department v. Yodell B.
key_cases.holding: The court held that ICWA's active efforts requirement under 25 U.S.C. Section 1912(d) must be proven by clear and convincing evidence and that the evidence at trial was insufficient, and it reversed the termination of the father's parental rights.
key_cases.relevance: Active efforts exist precisely to prevent the breakup of Indian families, and the court's insistence on proof is the enforcement mechanism.
key_cases.quote: the proper standard of proof for determinations under 25 U.S.C. § 1912(d) is the clear and convincing standard, which is applicable to the underlying termination of parental rights proceedings

key_cases.case_name: State ex rel. Children, Youth & Families Department v. Douglas B.
key_cases.holding: The Court held that a court must analyze a qualified expert witness's qualifications independently for each of ICWA's two required categories of testimony, and that the witness here was qualified as to tribal cultural standards but not as to serious emotional or physical damage, requiring a new adjudicatory hearing.
key_cases.relevance: Accepting an unqualified expert on serious damage to an Indian child is precisely the kind of ICWA shortfall that produces disparate removal outcomes for tribal families.
key_cases.quote: courts must independently analyze qualification in the two categories of required QEW testimony under ICWA and that the testimony can come from one or multiple experts

key_cases.case_name: State ex rel. Children, Youth & Families Department v. Casey J.
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed termination and held that CYFD's placement of the children complied with the Abuse and Neglect Act and ICWA because the record supported the district court's finding of good cause to deviate from the ICWA placement preferences, and that the father received due process.
key_cases.relevance: Good cause to deviate is the doctrine through which tribal placement preferences are most often defeated, so its contours are where disparate placement outcomes originate.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that the district court did not err in determining that good cause existed to deviate from the ICWA placement preferences at the time of the initial judicial review

key_cases.case_name: State ex rel. Children, Youth & Families Department v. Marlene C. (In re Esther V.)
key_cases.holding: The Court held that in a contested adjudication governed by ICWA the district court must always make the 25 U.S.C. Section 1912(d) and (e) findings at the adjudicatory stage, and separately held that New Mexico's ex parte and custody hearings are Section 1922 emergency proceedings to which Section 1912 does not apply; it reversed the neglect adjudication and remanded.
key_cases.relevance: ICWA's protections are the principal statutory guard in New Mexico against removal decisions that disregard a child's tribal identity.
key_cases.quote: in a contested adjudication to which ICWA applies, the district court must always make the findings of fact required under § 1912(d) and (e) of ICWA at the adjudication stage
